nodes.label: critic subagent
nodes.rationale: An Attacca-core subagent named `critic` that performs a fresh-context quality review of recent commits or the working diff. It looks for over-engineering, slop, redundancy, and commit claims the diff does not support, and is read-only: it reports, never edits.

nodes.label: Fresh-context reviewer stance
nodes.rationale: The agent reviews "with fresh eyes" — no attachment to the implementation and no memory of why it seemed necessary. The prompt states explicitly that this distance is the point of the agent.

nodes.label: Scan 1 — over-engineering
nodes.rationale: The first of three scans: abstractions with one caller, config for things that never vary, speculative generality ("we might need"), layers that only forward calls, and error handling for impossible states.

nodes.label: One-hour reimplementation test
nodes.rationale: The operational test for over-engineering: could a competent developer delete this and reimplement it in under an hour if it were actually needed? If so, it should not exist yet.

nodes.label: Scan 2 — slop
nodes.rationale: The second scan targets dead code, commented-out blocks, TODO litter, duplicate logic, naming inconsistent with the surrounding codebase, comments narrating the next line, and defensive re-validation of already-validated data.

nodes.label: Scan 3 — claims vs diff
nodes.rationale: The third scan reads the commit message(s) and asks whether the diff actually delivers what is claimed, whether stated non-goals are respected, and whether anything in the diff is unrelated to the stated purpose (scope creep).

nodes.label: Commit claims the diff does not support
nodes.rationale: The defect class of a commit message asserting something the diff does not deliver, plus violated non-goals and scope creep. An unsupported claim is explicitly a merge-blocking MUST finding.

nodes.label: Read-only: recommendations, never edits
nodes.rationale: The agent's hard refusal condition: it is read-only and produces recommendations, never edits. Stated twice — in the frontmatter description and as the first line of the Rules section.

nodes.label: Tool allowlist: Read, Bash, Grep, Glob
nodes.rationale: The frontmatter grants only Read, Bash, Grep, and Glob — inspection tools. No Write or Edit tool is granted, which is the mechanical counterpart to the read-only rule.

nodes.label: Model tier: sonnet
nodes.rationale: The frontmatter declares `model: sonnet` — a model tier rather than a dated model name, matching Attacca's convention for subagent frontmatter.

nodes.label: Every finding names file:line plus an alternative
nodes.rationale: A rule on findings: every one must name a `file:line` anchor and a concrete simpler alternative. A criticism without both is not a valid finding.

nodes.label: MUST / SHOULD / CONSIDER severity tiers
nodes.rationale: Findings are graded into three tiers: MUST blocks merge (an unsupported claim, dead code shipping), SHOULD is simplification, and CONSIDER is taste.

nodes.label: CRITIC REVIEW output block
nodes.rationale: The final message must be a fixed block: a `CRITIC REVIEW — [scope]` header, a VERDICT line, a `---` separator, then MUST / SHOULD / CONSIDER lines each shaped `[file:line] — [finding] → [simpler alternative]`.

nodes.label: VERDICT: CLEAN | MINOR | NEEDS_REVISION
nodes.rationale: The output block carries exactly one of three verdict states — CLEAN, MINOR, or NEEDS_REVISION — as the reviewer's summary judgement on the reviewed scope.

nodes.label: /code-review's bug-focused lens
nodes.rationale: The native `/code-review` focuses on bugs. The critic is positioned as complementary to it, supplying a "should this code exist at all" lens rather than a correctness one.

nodes.label: Use after implementing, before pushing
nodes.rationale: The declared invocation window: run the critic after implementing a feature and before pushing, over recent commits or the working diff.

nodes.label: Delete-when retirement condition
nodes.rationale: An HTML comment records the agent's own retirement trigger: delete it when native /code-review reliably flags over-engineering and unsupported commit claims, not just bugs.

nodes.label: researcher subagent
nodes.rationale: A subagent named `researcher` that performs web research in an isolated context — market/competitive analysis, library comparisons, API/docs lookups, best-practice surveys. Its system prompt opens 'You are a researcher. Your context is disposable — read widely here so the main conversation doesn't have to.'

nodes.label: disposable isolated context
nodes.rationale: The researcher's context window is declared disposable: it is expected to read widely inside its own isolated context, and nothing but its final message survives back to the caller.

nodes.label: keeping the main conversation lean
nodes.rationale: The stated purpose of delegating research is to keep the main conversation lean — the bulk reading happens in the subagent 'so the main conversation doesn't have to'.

nodes.label: invoke past 2-3 web fetches
nodes.rationale: The frontmatter description sets an explicit invocation threshold: 'Use whenever answering requires more than 2-3 web fetches.' Below that threshold the main conversation handles the lookup itself.

nodes.label: model tier: sonnet
nodes.rationale: The frontmatter pins `model: sonnet` — a model tier rather than a dated model name, per the repo's rule that subagent frontmatter uses tiers (`sonnet`/`haiku`).

nodes.label: read-only tool allowlist
nodes.rationale: The agent is granted exactly five tools — WebSearch, WebFetch, Read, Grep, Glob. All are read/fetch tools; no write, edit, or execution tool is granted, so the agent cannot change the repository.

nodes.label: four-step research method
nodes.rationale: The `## Method` section prescribes a four-step loop: decompose the question, search with a primary-source preference, cross-check load-bearing claims, then stop at saturation.

nodes.label: decompose into 2-5 sub-questions
nodes.rationale: Step 1 of the method: decompose the question into 2-5 searchable sub-questions. The bounded count both forces breakdown and caps the search surface.

nodes.label: primary sources and recency
nodes.rationale: Step 2: search each sub-question, preferring primary sources (official docs, changelogs, repos) over blog commentary, and note publication dates because recency matters.

nodes.label: cross-check load-bearing claims
nodes.rationale: Step 3: cross-check load-bearing claims against at least two independent sources, and explicitly flag anything that remains single-sourced rather than silently reporting it as established.

nodes.label: stop at search saturation
nodes.rationale: Step 4 gives the loop its termination rule: stop when additional searches only repeat what is already known. Saturation, not a fixed search budget, ends the run.

nodes.label: final message is the only deliverable
nodes.rationale: The reporting contract is that the agent's final message IS its only deliverable ('Output (final message — it is your only deliverable)'), returning findings with source URLs. Nothing is written to disk or handed back by any other channel.

nodes.label: lead with the direct answer
nodes.rationale: First element of the output contract: lead with the direct answer to the question that was asked, before any supporting detail.

nodes.label: findings grouped by sub-question with URLs
nodes.rationale: Second element of the output contract: findings grouped by sub-question, each carrying inline source URLs so every claim is traceable to where it came from.

nodes.label: confidence & gaps note
nodes.rationale: Third element: a short 'confidence & gaps' note stating what is well-supported, what is thin, and what changed recently enough that it should be re-verified later.

nodes.label: raw data over polish
nodes.rationale: Fourth element and a role boundary: return raw data rather than polished prose — 'the caller synthesizes'. Synthesis is explicitly outside the researcher's job.

nodes.label: caller owns synthesis
nodes.rationale: The division of labour puts synthesis with the calling conversation, not the researcher: the researcher gathers and cites, the caller draws the conclusion.

nodes.label: Delete when: marker
nodes.rationale: The file carries an HTML-comment retirement condition: 'Delete when: native deep-research workflows make ad-hoc research subagents redundant for small lookups.' It names in advance the future in which this agent should be removed.

nodes.label: csr-engine single Rust binary
nodes.rationale: The whole of Claude Self-Reflect v8.0 ships as one 44MB Rust binary called `csr-engine`: no Python, no Docker, no Qdrant. Every subsystem (MCP server, embeddings, search, storage, AST analysis, hooks, enrichment) lives inside that single process.

nodes.label: Embedded MCP server (rmcp, 15 tools)
nodes.rationale: The binary's default mode is an MCP server built on the `rmcp` crate (1.6) exposing 15 tools. All 15 declare `annotations(...)` in the tool macro, and params use the `Parameters<MyStruct>` pattern rather than individual `#[tool(param)]` arguments.

nodes.label: Local FastEmbed embeddings (384-dim)
nodes.rationale: Embeddings are produced locally by FastEmbed (crate `fastembed` 5.9) at 384 dimensions, so retrieval needs no remote embedding service. FastEmbed requires an aarch64 Rust toolchain (no x86_64-apple-darwin ONNX binaries), and `EmbeddingEngine::embed` takes `&mut self` so it is wrapped in a Mutex.

nodes.label: HNSW vector search (<1ms p95)
nodes.rationale: Search is an in-process HNSW index (crate `hnsw_rs` 0.3) with a stated p95 latency under 1ms, replacing the external Qdrant vector database of the v7 stack.

nodes.label: SQLite storage layer
nodes.rationale: Persistence is SQLite via `rusqlite` 0.38, including an FTS5 `chunks_fts` table and a `narrative_usage` table. Thread safety is obtained by wrapping the `Connection` in a `std::sync::Mutex`, and `usize` values must be cast to `i64` because rusqlite 0.38 has no `ToSql` for `usize`.

nodes.label: AST analysis via ast-grep (6 languages)
nodes.rationale: The engine embeds `ast-grep-core` 0.40 for AST analysis across 6 languages. It powers the `csr-engine quality <file>` code-quality command and supplies the AST anchors that tie conversations to specific functions and files.

nodes.label: 6 Claude Code hooks
nodes.rationale: Six Claude Code hooks fire at strategic moments (SessionStart, UserPromptSubmit, PostToolUse, Stop, PreCompact, SessionEnd), each dispatched through the same binary via `csr-engine hook <name>`. They are how capture and re-injection happen without the user invoking a tool.

nodes.label: 3-layer enrichment pipeline
nodes.rationale: The architecture diagram lists a 3-layer enrichment pipeline as a first-class component of csr-engine, alongside the MCP server, embeddings, search, storage, AST analysis and hooks. Background enrichment (including AI narratives) is driven by the daemon.

nodes.label: Multi-source corpus ingestion
nodes.rationale: From v9.4 the corpus is assembled from several distinct sources, each with its own ingestion stage: conversation transcripts (import watcher), task state (Stop hook), plan documents (30-minute daemon) and shell/session history (10-minute daemon). Each source carries its own `source=` tag so search can discriminate between them.

nodes.label: Conversation transcripts (~/.claude/projects/*.jsonl)
nodes.rationale: The primary corpus is Claude Code's own transcripts at `~/.claude/projects/*.jsonl`, ingested by an import watcher and tagged `source='conversation'`. The same files are what the Rust binary re-imports when upgrading from the v7 Python stack.

nodes.label: Task state (~/.claude/tasks/<session>/)
nodes.rationale: `~/.claude/tasks/<session>/` is treated as the authoritative task state and is ingested at the Stop hook, becoming an episode's todos and outcome. This is the outcome signal — what was actually attempted and whether it completed — rather than the narrative text of the conversation.

nodes.label: resolution_proposals (human-in-the-loop)
nodes.rationale: Completed tasks that match chunks still carrying a `still_open` verdict become `resolution_proposals` rather than auto-resolving. A human promotes a proposal to a verdict via the `csr_resolve` tool, so the system proposes closure but never asserts it unilaterally.

nodes.label: Plan documents (~/.claude/plans/*.md)
nodes.rationale: Plan markdown at `~/.claude/plans/*.md` is picked up by a 30-minute daemon pass, tagged `source='plan'` with `conversation_id=plan:<slug>`. Correlation to a conversation is margin-verified; ambiguous plans fall back to `_unscoped`, and a plan decays by its mtime timestamp rather than a conversation timestamp.

nodes.label: session_registry spine (~/.claude/history.jsonl)
nodes.rationale: `~/.claude/history.jsonl` is ingested by a 10-minute daemon pass as the `session_registry` spine — a structural index of sessions that is explicitly NEVER embedded and never injected into context. Its coverage is reported in `csr-engine status`.

nodes.label: Deliberate non-goals: memories and paste-cache
nodes.rationale: Memories and the paste-cache are explicitly NOT indexed, listed as deliberate non-goals for two reasons: circularity (indexing the system's own memory output feeds it back to itself) and privacy. Stating them as non-goals stops them being read as an omission.

nodes.label: aux_schema_miss:* adapter-drift counters
nodes.rationale: `aux_schema_miss:*` counters surfaced in `csr-engine status` flag adapter parse failures, i.e. an auxiliary source whose on-disk format the engine no longer understands. They are the thing to check when Claude Code renames an internal format — the TodoWrite→TaskCreate rename is the cited precedent.

nodes.label: Outcome-aware ranking and dedupe
nodes.rationale: Search results are ranked by what later happened to them, not just similarity: chunks whose verdict is `resolved` are demoted and annotated in future searches; the origin conversation always beats the derived plan in dedupe; and plan-sourced material decays on its own mtime timestamp.

nodes.label: csr_reflect_on_past
nodes.rationale: The headline MCP tool: semantic search across past conversations. It is the primary read surface over the indexed corpus and the tool the whole reflection loop exists to feed.

nodes.label: store_reflection
nodes.rationale: The one explicit write tool in the MCP surface: store an insight now so a future session can retrieve it. Everything else in the corpus arrives by passive capture; this is the deliberate, agent-authored memory.

nodes.label: csr_why — provenance chain
nodes.rationale: `csr_why` answers 'why does this code or decision exist' by returning a provenance chain, described as reinstatement recall — reconstructing the original decision context rather than returning topically similar text.

nodes.label: csr_resolve — verdict recording
nodes.rationale: `csr_resolve` records a verified verdict — `resolved`, `still_open` or `regressed` — against a chunk. It is the mechanism by which past outcomes are scored, and a `resolved` verdict subsequently demotes and annotates that chunk in searches.

nodes.label: csr_code_graph — conversations that shaped code
nodes.rationale: `csr_code_graph` answers which conversations shaped a given function or file, joining the transcript corpus to code through AST anchors rather than through filename string matching.

nodes.label: get_session_learnings — iteration memory
nodes.rationale: `get_session_learnings` exposes iteration memory, explicitly for Ralph loops — a long-running agent loop reading back what earlier iterations of itself learned, so each pass is not blind to the last.

nodes.label: Faceted search/retrieval tool family
nodes.rationale: Beyond plain semantic search, the MCP surface offers facets over the same corpus: `csr_quick_check` (fast existence check), `search_by_recency`, `get_recent_work` (session-grouped), `get_timeline` (stats), `csr_search_by_file`, `csr_search_by_concept`, `csr_search_insights` (aggregated patterns), `csr_get_more` (pagination) and `get_full_conversation` (complete JSONL).

nodes.label: SessionStart — past context as history
nodes.rationale: The SessionStart hook injects past context at the start of a session, and the design decision is recorded in the framing: it is presented as history, NOT as instructions, so recalled material informs the agent without commanding it.

nodes.label: UserPromptSubmit — predictive injection
nodes.rationale: The UserPromptSubmit hook fires on every prompt and performs predictive context injection — surfacing relevant past material automatically instead of waiting for the model to decide to call a search tool.

nodes.label: PostToolUse — file-change tracking
nodes.rationale: The PostToolUse hook fires after Edit/Write and tracks file changes, which is what lets conversations later be located by the files they touched.

nodes.label: Stop hook — iteration learnings + task capture
nodes.rationale: The Stop hook fires on every response and stores iteration learnings; it is also the ingestion stage at which `~/.claude/tasks/<session>/` task state is read into the corpus as episode todos and outcome.

nodes.label: PreCompact — state backup
nodes.rationale: The PreCompact hook backs up state before Claude Code compacts the conversation, so material that compaction would discard is captured to durable storage first.

nodes.label: SessionEnd — narrative storage
nodes.rationale: The SessionEnd hook stores a narrative of the session — a condensed account of what happened, which is the artifact the AI-narrative enrichment produces and which later retrieval surfaces.

nodes.label: Invariant: hooks never block Claude Code
nodes.rationale: All hooks use catch-all wrappers and must never block Claude Code. The reflection layer is strictly additive: a failure inside capture or injection degrades recall but must never break the host session.

nodes.label: AI narratives via `claude -p`
nodes.rationale: The only LLM-spending part of the system: narratives are generated by shelling out to `claude -p`, with a model chain of `CSR_NARRATIVE_MODEL` → `haiku` → the CLI default. Usage is counted in a `narrative_usage` table and shown in `csr-engine status`, and `CSR_NO_AI_NARRATIVES=1` is the kill switch.

nodes.label: Background enrichment daemon
nodes.rationale: `csr-engine daemon` runs background enrichment (AI narratives) and owns the periodic ingestion passes: plans every 30 minutes, `history.jsonl` every 10 minutes. It also refreshes the cached integrity check so the hot path never pays for it.

nodes.label: Cached integrity check
nodes.rationale: A raw `PRAGMA integrity_check` costs ~10s of CPU on multi-GB databases and must never run on the hot path; `Storage::integrity_check_cached` reads a meta-table cache that the daemon refreshes instead. Relatedly, macOS system sqlite3 cannot load fts5, so CLI inspection silently skips `chunks_fts` and looks ~10x faster than the bundled engine — use `csr-engine status --deep` or Homebrew sqlite3.

nodes.label: csr-engine status
nodes.rationale: `csr-engine status` emits JSON system status (with `--compact` for a statusline and `--deep` for a real integrity inspection). It is the single observability surface: registry coverage, `aux_schema_miss:*` adapter-drift counters, and AI-narrative usage all report there.

nodes.label: Built-in eval suite
nodes.rationale: The binary carries its own evaluation harness: `csr-engine eval` runs 5 tests in about 7ms and `csr-engine eval --full` runs 20 tests in about 200ms, making a retrieval-quality check cheap enough to run routinely rather than only in CI.

nodes.label: csr-engine setup (import + register + install)
nodes.rationale: `csr-engine setup` performs the three activation steps at once: import the existing corpus, register the MCP server, and install the hooks. `csr-engine hook install --apply` re-runs or updates just the hook installation.

nodes.label: Install and activation are separate consent steps
nodes.rationale: From v9.3.1 install and activation are deliberately separate consent steps: npm postinstall is download-only and the installer prompts before running `csr-engine setup`. `CSR_AUTO_SETUP=1` and `CSR_SKIP_SETUP=1` (install.sh only) override the prompt.

nodes.label: v7.x Python/Docker/Qdrant stack (replaced)
nodes.rationale: v8.0 replaced the entire v7.x Python + Docker + Qdrant stack. The upgrade is `docker compose down` then the install script; the Rust binary re-imports from the same `~/.claude/projects/` JSONL files, and `csr-engine hook install --apply` auto-replaces the Python hooks with Rust ones.

nodes.label: Critical operating rules
nodes.rationale: Five numbered critical rules govern agent work in the repo: use absolute `/Users/username/...` paths never `~/...` in MCP commands; never claim success without `cargo test`; restart Claude Code after modifying MCP server code; fix rather than bypass a blocking pre-commit hook; and drive tasks to completion.

nodes.label: GOAL-SEEKING RULE
nodes.rationale: Drive tasks to completion and never end a turn with a decision punt ('One thing I need from you', 'your call', option menus for routine choices). Make routine judgment calls yourself and state them; ask only for destructive or irreversible actions, spend, publish/release, or genuine scope changes.

nodes.label: QUALITY GATE rule
nodes.rationale: When the pre-commit hook blocks a commit, fix the underlying issue — never use `--no-verify`. Paired with the TEST RULE (never claim success without running `cargo test`) over a suite of 615 unit, 45 hooks-integration and 61 integration tests.

nodes.label: Claude Self-Reflect (CSR)
nodes.rationale: A local-first memory system for Claude Code whose stated purpose is 'Claude forgets everything. This fixes that.' It ships as a single 44MB binary with no databases, no containers and no API keys required, and gives Claude recall of past conversations.

nodes.label: The forgetting problem
nodes.rationale: Claude starts fresh every session, so solutions, architectures and debugged bugs are lost. The README quantifies it: context retention drops below 20% after 10 sessions.

nodes.label: Automatic context injection (no syntax)
nodes.rationale: The claimed user-facing guarantee: no special syntax and no commands — install once and relevant past context appears automatically when needed, found and injected by CSR rather than requested explicitly.

nodes.label: Single 44MB binary, one process
nodes.rationale: Everything runs locally in a single process of a 44MB binary: no Docker, no database server, no API keys required. This is the architectural commitment the rest of the design follows from.

nodes.label: v8.0 Rust rewrite
nodes.rationale: v8.0 replaced the earlier Python/Docker stack with a single Rust binary. Existing conversation data under ~/.claude/projects/ is untouched; the new engine re-imports from the same JSONL files.

nodes.label: Zero external dependencies
nodes.rationale: A headline guarantee of v9.4: zero external dependencies, backed by 720+ tests. No database server, no container runtime and no API key is needed for the core memory path.

nodes.label: SQLite storage layer
nodes.rationale: SQLite is the embedded store for chunks, embeddings and enrichment state — the persistence layer that lets the whole system be one process with no database server.

nodes.label: HNSW vector search
nodes.rationale: HNSW provides sub-millisecond vector search, claimed at <1ms p95. It is the retrieval index over the locally computed embeddings.

nodes.label: FastEmbed local embeddings
nodes.rationale: FastEmbed computes 384-dimension embeddings locally at a measured 0.73ms per text in batch, which is what removes the need for any embedding API key.

nodes.label: AST code-aware search
nodes.rationale: AST analysis gives code-aware search across 6 languages, producing the code anchors that let conversations be linked to specific functions and files.

nodes.label: Claimed performance profile
nodes.rationale: The stated numbers: ~150ms cached startup (p50 on a 54K-chunk index), <1ms p95 search latency, 44MB binary, ~20 conversations/sec import, 0.73ms/text embedding. First startup is slower (~14s for index rebuild).

nodes.label: Six session-lifecycle hooks
nodes.rationale: Six hooks fire across the Claude Code session lifecycle. They are the ambient half of the mechanism — memory is captured and re-surfaced without the user issuing any command.

nodes.label: SessionStart hook
nodes.rationale: Surfaces relevant past context at the start of a conversation, which is the first point at which the forgetting problem would otherwise bite.

nodes.label: UserPromptSubmit hook
nodes.rationale: Predicts and injects context before Claude responds — predictive rather than requested retrieval, fired on every prompt.

nodes.label: PostToolUse hook
nodes.rationale: Tracks file edits with session-scoped deduplication, which is what supplies the file-to-conversation association used by file and code-graph searches.

nodes.label: Stop hook
nodes.rationale: Stores iteration learnings on every response and detects stuck patterns — the iteration-level memory that `get_session_learnings` later reads for Ralph loops.

nodes.label: PreCompact hook
nodes.rationale: Backs up state before context compaction, so material about to be dropped from the live context window is captured into durable memory first.

nodes.label: SessionEnd hook
nodes.rationale: Stores a session narrative for future retrieval, closing the capture loop so the next session's SessionStart has something to surface.

nodes.label: Hooks never block Claude Code
nodes.rationale: A stated safety guarantee: all hooks use catch-all error handling and never block Claude Code, so a memory-layer failure degrades recall rather than breaking the host agent.

nodes.label: 15 MCP tools for explicit search
nodes.rationale: Fifteen MCP tools give Claude explicit, model-invoked access to the memory store — semantic search, recency and timeline queries, file/concept search, pagination, full-conversation retrieval, provenance and verdict recording. This is the deliberate half of the mechanism, complementing the automatic hooks.

nodes.label: MCP tool safety annotations
nodes.rationale: All tools carry MCP tool annotations so Claude Code understands their safety characteristics. Thirteen are read-only; only `store_reflection` and `csr_resolve` write.

nodes.label: csr_reflect_on_past
nodes.rationale: The primary read-only tool: semantic search across past conversations. It is the direct-recall entry point that the specialised tools (recency, file, concept, insights) narrow.

nodes.label: store_reflection (writes)
nodes.rationale: One of only two writing tools: stores insights for future retrieval, letting the agent deliberately deposit a lesson rather than relying on the ambient hook capture.

nodes.label: csr_code_graph
nodes.rationale: Links code symbols to the conversations that shaped them, answering 'which conversations shaped this function or file' via AST anchors. Called out in the README as a distinguishing tool.

nodes.label: csr_why (provenance chain)
nodes.rationale: Returns a provenance chain answering why a piece of code or a decision exists — the tool-level expression of the paper's intent-over-similarity retrieval design.

nodes.label: csr_resolve (verified verdicts)
nodes.rationale: The second writing tool: records verified verdicts (resolved / still_open / regressed) on chunks, so stored memory carries an explicit truth status rather than only a similarity score.

nodes.label: Three-layer progressive enrichment pipeline
nodes.rationale: Three layers progressively improve search quality from raw chunks to AI-enriched narratives, claimed as a 9.3x improvement. The stated payoff is higher-quality context, better decisions and fewer tokens.

nodes.label: AI narratives (optional top layer)
nodes.rationale: An optional background daemon that transforms raw conversations into rich searchable narratives, raising measured search quality from 0.074 to 0.691 — the 9.3x figure. It is opt-in and disableable with CSR_NO_AI_NARRATIVES=1.

nodes.label: Optional Anthropic dependency for narratives
nodes.rationale: The one place the no-API-key claim is relaxed: AI narratives require an Anthropic API key, cost roughly $0.012 per conversation via the Batch API, and run `claude -p` against an existing Claude subscription using the smallest available model with capped, debounced prompts.

nodes.label: 82% token compression
nodes.rationale: With AI narratives, injected context drops to 18% of the raw token count — an 82% reduction — so better recall is claimed to cost fewer tokens, not more.

nodes.label: Token-spend transparency
nodes.rationale: Every narrative call — including failures and timeouts — is counted. `csr-engine status` shows calls and tokens spent today, and cache read/creation tokens (often the majority of real usage) are tracked separately as cache_tokens_today / cache_tokens_total.

nodes.label: Preprint: Similarity Drowns Intent
nodes.rationale: 'Similarity Drowns Intent: Three-Trace Sagas and Reinstatement Recall for Provenance in Agentic Software Construction' (2026) documents CSR's retrieval design, measured on the system's own development history.

nodes.label: Similarity drowns intent (failure mode)
nodes.rationale: Ask a memory system 'why did we drop Qdrant?' and cosine similarity returns a recording of you asking that same question earlier at 0.984 similarity: the decision itself scores lower than its own echoes. Pure similarity retrieval surfaces restatements of the query instead of its answer.

nodes.label: Multi-hop walk over one-shot kNN
nodes.rationale: The countermeasure the paper measures: a multi-hop walk that beat one-shot kNN by +53% and +47% ground-truth session coverage on two corpora, under pre-registered gates and blind cross-vendor judging.

nodes.label: Self-recording memory contaminates its own eval
nodes.rationale: A second finding that fell out of evaluation: a self-recording memory system ingests its own eval dialogue and then drowns the very answers it is being tested on.

nodes.label: Kept negative results (ratification weighting)
nodes.rationale: The paper keeps its negative results: a pre-registered ratification-weighting hypothesis died at rho ~= 0 and thereby forbade an entire staleness design.

nodes.label: Multi-source memory (v9.4)
nodes.rationale: v9.4 widened the corpus beyond transcripts to task outcomes, plan documents and a cross-project session registry — each absorbed at the lifecycle stage it belongs to rather than through one uniform importer.

nodes.label: Episodes carrying real task state
nodes.rationale: Episodes carry real task state again: Claude Code's TodoWrite -> TaskCreate rename had silently emptied them. A host-side format rename is thus a live failure mode for any memory layer parsing the host's internal artifacts.

nodes.label: Schema-miss telemetry
nodes.rationale: The guard added after the silent-emptying bug: schema-miss telemetry, so a future adapter parse failure is reported rather than degrading into quietly empty memory.

nodes.label: Consent-first activation
nodes.rationale: Downloading the (SHA256-verified) binary and activating it are separate consent steps: registering the MCP server, installing the hooks and importing conversations only run with explicit consent, and non-interactive installs never activate on their own.

nodes.label: Three-Tier Fable 5 Orchestrator Workflow
nodes.rationale: Split one coding task across three models instead of running everything on one: Fable 5 is the lead that plans and makes judgment calls, Opus takes the hard reasoning steps, Sonnet handles the boilerplate. Motivation is cost: Fable spends its tokens only where the quality difference shows up in the output, while Sonnet absorbs the volume of mechanical work at a fraction of the per-token cost. Set up with two built-in Claude Code commands and one text file; takes about ten minutes. Uses Anthropic models only - no third-party CLI or plugin.

nodes.label: Fable 5 (orchestrator tier)
nodes.rationale: Anthropic's most capable model, $10 input / $50 output per MTok - roughly 2x Opus 4.8 and 3-5x Sonnet 5. Launched June 2026 and designed to dispatch and manage subagents more reliably than earlier Claude models, which is why this pattern picked up traction. In this workflow it is the orchestrator only: plan, decompose, synthesize.

nodes.label: Opus 4.8 (deep-reasoning tier)
nodes.rationale: $5 input / $25 output per MTok - half Fable 5's rate. Bound to the deep-reasoner subagent for the hard reasoning steps. Also the model Claude Code silently reroutes a Fable session to when a safety classifier trips, and the substitute orchestrator for anyone without Fable 5 access.

nodes.label: Sonnet 5 (mechanical tier)
nodes.rationale: Intro pricing $2 input / $10 output per MTok through Aug 31, 2026; standard pricing $3 input / $15 output per MTok after that. Bound to the fast-worker subagent and absorbs the volume of mechanical work.

nodes.label: Model Tier Pricing Table ($/MTok)
nodes.rationale: Fable 5: $10 in / $50 out. Opus 4.8: $5 in / $25 out. Sonnet 5 intro (through Aug 31, 2026): $2 in / $10 out. Sonnet 5 standard (after Aug 31, 2026): $3 in / $15 out. Stated as current API rates at time of writing.

nodes.label: Output Tokens Are Where the Tier Gap Bites
nodes.rationale: Output tokens carry the widest multiple: every plan or explanation Fable writes costs 5x what the same text would cost from Sonnet at intro pricing ($50 vs $10 per MTok). This is why the split targets who WRITES, not just who thinks - the orchestrator must keep its own output short and push volume production down-tier.

nodes.label: Subscription Usage Multiplier for Fable Sessions
nodes.rationale: The gap is not only an API line item. On a Claude.ai subscription, Claude Code's model picker labels Fable sessions as consuming roughly double the usage against session and weekly limits compared to an equivalent Opus session, and several times more than Sonnet. Routing a long refactor entirely through Fable burns the usage window on work that never needed frontier-level judgment.

nodes.label: deep-reasoner Subagent
nodes.rationale: Recovered code block 2 (Step 3a), verbatim: "Create a subagent called deep-reasoner. Model: opus. Description: Use for reasoning-heavy phases, architecture, debugging complex issues, algorithm design. Think thoroughly, return a concise conclusion the orchestrator can act on." The instruction to return a CONCISE conclusion is a context-budget device: the deep tier may think at length but must hand back something small the orchestrator can act on without absorbing the reasoning.

nodes.label: fast-worker Subagent
nodes.rationale: Recovered code block 3 (Step 3b), verbatim: "Create a subagent called fast-worker. Model: sonnet. Description:\"Use for mechanical tasks, boilerplate, tests, formatting, simple edits. Execute efficiently.\"" No thinking instruction at all - the contrast with deep-reasoner's "think thoroughly" is the whole tier distinction.

nodes.label: Model Binding: deep-reasoner = opus
nodes.rationale: Stated in the author's own words as "Model: opus" inside the subagent-creation prompt. The binding is per-ROLE, not per-session: the orchestrator stays on Fable while this subagent runs on Opus, so reasoning-heavy phases cost Opus rates rather than Fable rates. A subagent's model assignment is separate from any reusable instructions it draws on.

nodes.label: Model Binding: fast-worker = sonnet
nodes.rationale: Stated in the author's own words as "Model: sonnet" inside the subagent-creation prompt. Mechanical tasks, boilerplate, tests, formatting and simple edits execute at Sonnet rates - the volume tier - while the Fable orchestrator never writes that output itself.

nodes.label: CLAUDE.md Orchestration Block
nodes.rationale: Recovered code block 4 (Step 4), verbatim: "#Orchestration workflow / You (Fable) are the orchestrator. Plan, decompose, synthesize. Reasoning-heavy phases go to deep-reasoner (Opus). Mechanical work goes to fast-worker (Sonnet). For high-stakes decisions, run deep-reasoner twice with slightly different framings and synthesize the best of both. Keep your own context lean. Delegate rather than doing mechanical work yourself." This block is the whole routing policy; the article's FAQ notes the same block works unchanged with Opus as orchestrator.

nodes.label: Run deep-reasoner Twice With Different Framings
nodes.rationale: Verbatim from the CLAUDE.md block: "For high-stakes decisions, run deep-reasoner twice with slightly different framings and synthesize the best of both." A cheap ensemble at the reasoning tier - two Opus passes still cost less than one Fable pass of the same length, and the orchestrator's job on high-stakes calls becomes synthesis rather than original reasoning.

nodes.label: Keep Your Own Context Lean
nodes.rationale: Verbatim directive to the orchestrator: "Keep your own context lean." Because the orchestrator is the most expensive tier, every token it re-reads is billed at frontier rates; subagents absorb the bulky reading and return conclusions.

nodes.label: Delegate Rather Than Doing Mechanical Work Yourself
nodes.rationale: Verbatim directive closing the CLAUDE.md block: "Delegate rather than doing mechanical work yourself." Stated as a standing default rather than a per-task judgment, because the failure mode is the orchestrator quietly doing a small edit itself at frontier rates.

nodes.label: Per-Task Prompt Shape (Goal / Context / Lead)
nodes.rationale: Recovered code block 5 (Step 5), verbatim: "Goal: [what you want] / Context: [files, constraints] / You're the lead. Delegate reasoning to deep-reasoner, grunt work to fast-worker. Show me your plan first, then execute." Brief the orchestrator like a tech lead briefing a senior engineer, not a single instruction to execute directly.

nodes.label: Show Me Your Plan First, Then Execute
nodes.rationale: Verbatim from the per-task prompt. Fable typically responds with a breakdown of the task before touching any code, which gives the human a chance to redirect it before it spends tokens on the wrong approach - a cost control, not just a review habit.

nodes.label: Launch Command (cd to project, run claude)
nodes.rationale: Recovered code block 1 (Step 1), verbatim: "cd path/to/your/project claude" - i.e. change into the project folder and start a Claude Code session there. Everything in the setup happens inside that one session.

nodes.label: .claude/agents/ Subagent Directory
nodes.rationale: Subagent definitions are markdown files in the project's .claude/agents/ directory. Option A has Claude write them for you from a prompt; Option B (recommended by the article) is writing the files by hand, because that is what allows customisation to project needs.

nodes.label: .claude/agents/deep-reasoner.md
nodes.rationale: The hand-written file path named explicitly in Step 3 Option B for the Opus-bound reasoning subagent.

nodes.label: .claude/agents/fast-worker.md
nodes.rationale: The sibling hand-written file for the Sonnet-bound mechanical subagent ("Similarly for the fast-worker file").

nodes.label: Project-Root CLAUDE.md File
nodes.rationale: A plain text file named exactly CLAUDE.md in the root of the project folder; Claude Code reads it automatically at the start of every session in that folder. The article keeps its example minimal for tutorial purposes and states that a fuller CLAUDE.md matters for efficiency.

nodes.label: /model Command
nodes.rationale: Step 2: type /model, select Fable 5 to set the session's main model. Also the manual recovery path after a safety-classifier reroute (/model fable).

nodes.label: /agents Command
nodes.rationale: Creates, edits and removes subagents; can be re-run at any point to add more. The CLAUDE.md block can reference as many agents as are defined.

nodes.label: /effort high
nodes.rationale: Step 2 sets reasoning effort to high, not max. One builder testing Fable 5 across a full day found max effort burned through tokens fast for output that was not actually better than high; high is the model's own default and the recommended starting point.

nodes.label: Effort Level Drives Cost
nodes.rationale: FAQ: higher effort settings mean more tokens spent per response. high is a reasonable default; reserve max for problems where the extra reasoning has been confirmed to change the output.

nodes.label: Restart the Session After Adding Agent Files
nodes.rationale: New agent files placed in a directory that did not exist when the session started are not picked up until the session restarts. A silent failure mode: the files exist, the delegation instructions exist, and nothing routes.

nodes.label: Safety-Classifier Silent Reroute to Opus 4.8
nodes.rationale: Fable 5 runs safety classifiers on cybersecurity and biology-related content. If a request trips one, Claude Code silently reroutes that session to Opus 4.8 and stays there until /model fable is run manually. Easy to miss because workspace context such as CLAUDE.md or git status can trip it on the very first message. If Fable seems to be responding differently than expected mid-project, check which model is actually active before assuming the setup is broken.

nodes.label: Fallback Structure Without Fable 5 Access
nodes.rationale: FAQ: the exact same structure runs with Opus as the orchestrator and Sonnet as the sole subagent. The delegation logic in CLAUDE.md stays the same - the policy is model-agnostic, only the tier assignment changes.

nodes.label: Community Pattern, Not an Official Anthropic Recommendation
nodes.rationale: FAQ, explicit: this is not an official Anthropic-recommended setup. It is a pattern shared by individual Claude Code users based on their own testing. Anthropic's documented pattern is similar in spirit - pairing a stronger model for planning with a cheaper one for execution - but this specific three-tier version comes from the community. Adapted from setups shared by builders on X.

nodes.label: Diego (@diegocabezas01) X Post
nodes.rationale: Named upstream source for the workflow: https://x.com/diegocabezas01/status/2072436501263339841

nodes.label: Scope Limit: Coding Projects Only
nodes.rationale: FAQ: subagents, CLAUDE.md and /agents are Claude Code features built specifically for coding projects, so this pattern does not transfer to writing or content work - that needs a different toolset.

nodes.label: Loop Engineering Design Patterns
nodes.rationale: Cited as the dynamic sibling of this workflow: this delegation logic is a simpler, STATIC version of loop engineering patterns, where an agent decides mid-task when to hand work to an evaluator. Positioned as the natural next step once the static setup feels comfortable.

nodes.label: carbon.now.sh Iframe Code-Block Extraction Loss
nodes.rationale: Appendix note added 2026-08-06. All five of the article's code blocks are not text in the page: each is a lazy-loaded carbon.now.sh iframe whose payload is DOUBLE-URL-encoded in the code= query parameter of its data-lazy-src attribute (%2523 -> %23 -> #). trafilatura extracts article text and does not decode iframe query strings, so the first fetch produced a body where "Paste this into it:" was followed by nothing. Distinct from the kb-add truncation defect (#200) - the prose body was complete. kb-fetch's roundtrip check did not catch it: it sampled 11 tokens and reported 0 missing while all 974 chars were absent. Control arm: advisor-executor-claude-code-fable5.md fetched the same way the same day retained 4 fenced code blocks, so trafilatura does preserve real pre/code content and the cause is the iframe embed, not the fetcher dropping code.

nodes.label: fable-advisor agent (second-opinion advisor)
nodes.rationale: The `fable-advisor` subagent is defined as a second-opinion advisor and final reviewer: 'the most capable model in this session, consulted sparingly, at exactly the moments that decide whether the next hour of work is wasted.' The caller passes it the decision (or the diff), the constraints, and the options considered, and it returns a verdict with reasoning and the risk that decides it. It advises only — it never implements.

nodes.label: model: fable (Claude's most capable model)
nodes.rationale: The agent's frontmatter declares `model: fable`, described as 'Claude's most capable model (Fable 5)'. The model choice is the whole point of the agent: it is the expensive, high-capability tier reserved for commitment boundaries rather than for routine work.

nodes.label: Read-only tool grant (Read, Grep, Glob)
nodes.rationale: The frontmatter grants exactly three tools: `Read, Grep, Glob`. No write, edit, or execution tool is granted, so the agent has read-only access to the codebase — the mechanical counterpart of the 'advises only' rule.

nodes.label: Occasion 1: commitment boundaries
nodes.rationale: The first of two occasions for consulting the advisor: 'an architecture choice, a data migration, an API shape, a refactor strategy, a debugging effort that has failed twice.' The consult happens *before* the orchestrator commits, so the advice can still change the decision.

nodes.label: Two-failed-attempts trigger
nodes.rationale: A specific, mechanical trigger for escalation: consult the advisor 'whenever the same problem has resisted two attempts' — i.e. a debugging effort that has failed twice. Two failures is the threshold at which continuing on the cheap lane is judged more expensive than paying for the advisor.

nodes.label: Occasion 2: end-of-deliverable final review
nodes.rationale: The advisor is called ALWAYS once at the end of a deliverable, before the orchestrator reports done, to review the accumulated changes — the diff, new files, touched tests — 'with fresh eyes and no accumulated conversational assumptions.'

nodes.label: Read the diff against the stated goal, not the conversation
nodes.rationale: The final-review method: read the diff against the stated goal rather than against the conversation, checking that nothing asked-for is missing and nothing unasked-for was smuggled in, that verification evidence is real, and that the diff creates no risk the orchestrator has not named.

nodes.label: Verdict: ship / fix these first / rethink
nodes.rationale: The review returns one of three verdicts: ship, fix these specific things first, or rethink. 'Ship' gets one line; problems must be named precisely with the file and the fix, in the same format as any other advisory answer.

nodes.label: How-to-answer protocol (five rules)
nodes.rationale: The agent definition prescribes a five-rule answering protocol: look before you opine, give a verdict not a survey, a sound plan gets one line, missing information is named precisely, and stay under ~300 words. Together they force advice dense enough for another model to act on mid-task.

nodes.label: Rule 1: look before you opine
nodes.rationale: 'You have read-only access to the codebase. If the decision depends on how the code actually works, read it — don't reason from the summary you were handed.' The advisor is required to verify against the source rather than trust the caller's framing.

nodes.label: Rule 2: a verdict, not a survey
nodes.rationale: The required answer shape is 'Do X, not Y, because Z' plus the single risk that decides it. 'If you're weighing options for more than a sentence, you're doing the caller's job instead of yours' — option-weighing belongs to the orchestrator, not the advisor.

nodes.label: Rule 3: a sound plan gets one line
nodes.rationale: When the plan is sound the answer is a single line — 'Plan is sound; the one thing to watch is X.' The definition explicitly forbids manufacturing objections to justify having been consulted.

nodes.label: Rule 4: name missing information precisely
nodes.rationale: If something the advisor does not have would change the answer, it must say exactly what that is and what each possible answer would imply. Hedging with 'it depends' is disallowed unless the dependency itself is stated.

nodes.label: Rule 5: stay under ~300 words
nodes.rationale: A hard length budget of roughly 300 words, justified by the reader: 'Your reader is another model mid-task, not a human reading a report.' The output is context injected into a working agent, so brevity is a cost constraint, not a style preference.

nodes.label: What the advisor never does
nodes.rationale: The definition closes with an explicit prohibition list under 'What you never do': never implement/edit/write files, never rubber-stamp, and never expand scope. These three are stated as absolutes rather than defaults.

nodes.label: Never implements, edits, or writes files
nodes.rationale: 'Implement, edit, or write files. You advise; the working model builds.' The description repeats it as 'Advises only — never implements.' The division of labour is explicit: the advisor decides, the cheaper working model types.

nodes.label: Never rubber-stamps
nodes.rationale: 'Rubber-stamp. If you'd genuinely push back, push back.' The advisor is forbidden from approving to be agreeable; a real objection must be voiced even when the caller clearly wants a green light.

nodes.label: Never expands scope
nodes.rationale: 'Expand scope. Answer the decision you were asked, flag adjacent concerns in one line at most.' Adjacent issues get at most a single line; the advisor answers the question posed rather than redefining the work.

nodes.label: Expensive and slow — that's the deal
nodes.rationale: 'You are expensive and slow relative to the models doing the typing — that's the deal. You're not here to help type; you're here to be right when it matters.' The cost asymmetry is the stated reason for consulting sparingly and only at decision points.

nodes.label: Codex Implementer Lane
nodes.rationale: The default implementation lane: a sonnet-model subagent (tools Bash, Read, Grep, Glob) that does not write code itself but delivers the spec to the Codex CLI, supervises the run, verifies the result, and reports. Routine, well-specified work is routed here because the spec fully determines the outcome.

nodes.label: GPT-5.6 Luna
nodes.rationale: The OpenAI model that actually writes the code in this lane, selected with `--model gpt-5.6-luna`. Luna supports reasoning efforts low/medium/high/xhigh/max — there is no `ultra` rung. If the model is unavailable to the account or workspace, the lane returns STATUS: unavailable with the exact access error.

nodes.label: OpenAI Codex CLI (codex exec)
nodes.rationale: The `codex exec` CLI is the transport for this lane; it must be installed and authenticated. It is invoked non-interactively with the prompt on stdin and the model's final message captured via `--output-last-message`.

nodes.label: Cross-family model diversity
nodes.rationale: The rationale for the lane: the typing runs on an independent model family from the session, because a second family catches what a single vendor's models jointly miss. The caller chooses this lane specifically for vendor diversity.

nodes.label: Architect stays Claude
nodes.rationale: The architect remains Claude while only the implementation typing is delegated to another vendor's model. This split is what makes the arrangement cross-family rather than a single-vendor pipeline.

nodes.label: Fraction of the architect's token cost
nodes.rationale: Codex does the typing at a fraction of the architect's token cost, which is the economic reason routine well-specified work is routed to this lane rather than kept in the architect session.

nodes.label: Preflight availability check
nodes.rationale: The lane's first action, always: `command -v codex && codex --version`. If codex is missing or unauthenticated the lane stops immediately rather than proceeding.

nodes.label: No silent fallback
nodes.rationale: The lane never implements the task itself as a fallback. A cross-vendor lane that quietly becomes a Claude lane is worse than a loud failure, so unavailability is reported as a structured error instead.

nodes.label: STATUS: unavailable
nodes.rationale: The report status returned when codex is not on PATH, auth fails, or gpt-5.6-luna is inaccessible to the account or workspace. REASON must preserve the exact error message.

nodes.label: Standard five-part spec
nodes.rationale: The contract for the prompt this lane receives: objective, files, interfaces, constraints, and a verification command. It is restated cleanly into the prompt file, ending with an instruction to run the verification command and include its actual output.

nodes.label: Spec-gap flagging
nodes.rationale: If parts of the five-part spec are missing, the lane passes the gap to codex as an explicit open question and flags it in the GAPS field of its report rather than guessing.

nodes.label: Unique mktemp prompt file
nodes.rationale: Step 1 of running codex: write the spec to a unique `mktemp` file (and a separate final-message file) — never inline shell quoting and never a fixed path.

nodes.label: Parallel-lane file corruption
nodes.rationale: The failure mode the unique prompt file exists to prevent: parallel lanes writing to fixed paths corrupt each other's spec and final-message files.

nodes.label: Lane opt-out preamble
nodes.rationale: A preamble prepended to the spec file stating that the model and reasoning effort named in the invocation were chosen deliberately, that this lane is an explicit opt-out from any instruction file mandating a different orchestration flow, and that every other instruction in those files still applies. It is belt-and-braces, not a substitute for checking the diff.

nodes.label: ~/.codex/AGENTS.md loaded every invocation
nodes.rationale: `codex exec` loads the user's `~/.codex/AGENTS.md` on every invocation, so a rule written for one project governs every lane on the machine. A rule pinning a model/effort or mandating an orchestration flow makes codex decline the work.

nodes.label: Silent refusal (exit 0, empty diff)
nodes.rationale: The observed failure mode (live, 2026-08-04): codex correctly declines rather than substituting, and the run returns exit 0 with an empty diff and a polite refusal in the final message. Nothing in the exit code reveals it — a silent success.

nodes.label: Non-negotiable flag discipline
nodes.rationale: The fixed set of flags every codex invocation in this lane must carry, each with a stated reason: sandbox scope, pinned reasoning effort, deterministic working root, stdin prompt delivery, and a wall-clock cap.

nodes.label: --sandbox workspace-write
nodes.rationale: Codex writes code scoped to the working tree. `danger-full-access` is never used in this lane.

nodes.label: -c model_reasoning_effort=max
nodes.rationale: Pins GPT-5.6 Luna to max reasoning — its top rung. The lane always runs the model at maximum effort rather than leaving it to a default.

nodes.label: --skip-git-repo-check + --cd $(pwd)
nodes.rationale: Together they give a deterministic working root and let the lane run outside git repositories.

nodes.label: Prompt via stdin (`- < spec file`)
nodes.rationale: The spec is delivered to codex on stdin from the temp file using the trailing `-`, which avoids quoting hazards and truncated specs.

nodes.label: Quoting hazards and truncated specs
nodes.rationale: The risk of passing a spec as an inline shell argument: shell quoting can mangle it and long specs can be truncated — which is why the prompt goes over stdin from a file.

nodes.label: Portable 10-minute timeout
nodes.rationale: `T=$(command -v gtimeout || command -v timeout || true)` then `${T:+$T 600}` gives a ten-minute wall clock where a timeout binary exists; macOS has none unless coreutils is installed, in which case the run is uncapped and a WARN is printed.

nodes.label: STATUS: timeout
nodes.rationale: On hitting the wall clock, the lane reports STATUS: timeout together with whatever work actually landed, rather than discarding the partial result.

nodes.label: Model slug is a default, not a constant
nodes.rationale: `--model gpt-5.6-luna` selects the Luna capability tier and is a documented default; if the caller's spec names a different codex model, the lane uses that instead.

nodes.label: Independent verification step
nodes.rationale: Step 3: read the diff (`git diff` / `git status`), re-run the spec's verification command yourself, and read codex's final message from the captured file. Completion is never claimed without the lane's own re-run.

nodes.label: Codex's claim is not evidence
nodes.rationale: "Codex said it works" is forbidden as evidence; only the lane's own re-run of the verification command counts. A clean exit code is likewise not evidence that work happened.

nodes.label: An empty diff is never `complete`
nodes.rationale: If codex exits 0 but `git diff` shows nothing changed, the lane returns STATUS: refused and quotes codex's final message verbatim in REASON. The empty diff is what actually catches a refusal, whatever caused it.

nodes.label: STATUS: refused
nodes.rationale: The report status for a run that exited cleanly but produced no change, carrying codex's refusal message verbatim so the caller can see why.

nodes.label: CODEX REPORT structure
nodes.rationale: The fixed return shape: STATUS (complete | partial | timeout | unavailable | refused), OBJECTIVE, CHANGES per file from the actual diff, VERIFIED with the re-run command's actual output, CODEX SAID (noting any disagreement with the diff), and GAPS.

nodes.label: One codex invocation per task
nodes.rationale: The lane makes exactly one codex invocation per task unless the caller has explicitly decomposed the work into parts.

nodes.label: Do not patch codex's wrong changes
nodes.rationale: If codex's changes are wrong, the lane reports that plainly with the failing output and does not fix them itself — fix decisions belong to the caller.

nodes.label: The calling architect
nodes.rationale: The upstream orchestrator that wrote the spec and chose this lane. Fix decisions and architectural decisions belong to it, not to the implementer lane.

nodes.label: Stop on an architectural problem
nodes.rationale: If the task turns out to be architectural — the spec itself is wrong — the lane stops and reports, because that decision belongs upstream and the advisor should be consulted.

nodes.label: fable-advisor consult
nodes.rationale: The advisory agent named as the escalation target when the spec itself is wrong and the problem is architectural rather than implementational.

nodes.label: Architect-as-orchestrator pattern
nodes.rationale: The session is the architect: it owns requirements, architecture, decomposition, specs, routing, and verification, and should almost never type implementation code. Every implementation task is routed to the cheapest adequate lane, and every finished deliverable gets a Fable review before the architect reports done.

nodes.label: Cost discipline (prime directive)
nodes.rationale: The prime directive of the pattern's economics: Opus orchestrates (judgment-heavy, volume-light), GPT-5.6 Luna does the routine typing (volume-heavy, cheap, cross-vendor), and Fable — the most expensive model available — is spent only where it changes outcomes: the hardest one-off implementations and the final review.

nodes.label: Emit judgment, not volume
nodes.rationale: The architect's output is decomposition, specs, routing decisions, verdicts on diffs, and short reports — not implementation code, test bodies, boilerplate, or config. A code block longer than an interface signature or a few illustrative lines is a spec that hasn't been delegated yet, and fixing a lane's bug by hand is the same failure in disguise.

nodes.label: Keep the context lean
nodes.rationale: Everything in the architect's context is re-read at architect prices on every turn, so broad exploration, codebase searches, and log-grepping are delegated to a cheap read-only agent and only the conclusions are kept. Read files yourself only when the decision genuinely depends on the exact code; never paste long files, full diffs, or verbose command output when a path reference or excerpt will do.

nodes.label: Reason once, then hand off
nodes.rationale: Do the hard thinking — architecture, interface design, the debugging hypothesis — in one pass, capture it in the spec, and let the lane carry it from there. Re-deriving decisions across turns burns the premium twice.

nodes.label: Work retained by the architect
nodes.rationale: Regardless of cost, these stay with the architect: decomposition, interface design, hypothesis selection when debugging, spec writing, lane routing, and judging verification evidence. Those tokens are what the premium is for; everything else is a candidate for delegation.

nodes.label: Routine lane (codex-implementer)
nodes.rationale: The default lane: GPT-5.6 Luna at max reasoning, invoked via the `codex-implementer` agent, used when the spec fully determines the outcome — boilerplate, wiring, CRUD, mechanical edits, straightforward features. It requires the codex CLI.

nodes.label: High-complexity lane (fable-implementer)
nodes.rationale: Fable 5 via the `fable-implementer` agent, routed to when the outcome depends heavily on judgment the spec can't capture: subtle concurrency, non-trivial algorithms, security-sensitive paths, hard debugging, wide-blast-radius refactors — or when the routine lane has already failed the task once. These are one-off escalations, never the default.

nodes.label: Review lane (fable-advisor)
nodes.rationale: The `fable-advisor` agent (Fable 5) is not an implementation lane: it is read-only and returns a verdict in under 300 words. It serves commitment boundaries and the mandatory end-of-deliverable review.

nodes.label: Lane deciding rule
nodes.rationale: The routing question is: how much does the outcome depend on judgment the spec can't capture? Little means the default codex lane (you will verify anyway); a lot, with costly mistakes, means escalate to `fable-implementer` or keep the piece with the architect.

nodes.label: Two-failure escalation rule
nodes.rationale: A routine-lane task that fails its spec once gets a corrected spec; failing twice escalates it to Fable. Repetition is evidence the task was misclassified.

nodes.label: Cross-vendor independence
nodes.rationale: The codex lane is the cross-vendor half of the pattern: its output comes from a non-Anthropic family, so the Claude architect's verification and the Fable review are genuine cross-vendor checks rather than same-family self-review.

nodes.label: Codex-lane unavailable fallback
nodes.rationale: If the codex lane returns `unavailable` or `timeout`, re-route the same spec to `fable-implementer` and say so explicitly in the report — never quietly absorb the substitution or the cost change.

nodes.label: The five-part spec contract
nodes.rationale: Implementers share none of the architect's conversation context, so every delegation prompt must carry all five parts: Objective, Files, Interfaces, Constraints, and Verification.

nodes.label: Spec part: Objective
nodes.rationale: Objective: what to build or change, stated in one paragraph.

nodes.label: Spec part: Files
nodes.rationale: Files: the exact paths the implementer is to create or modify.

nodes.label: Spec part: Interfaces
nodes.rationale: Interfaces: the signatures, types, or API shapes the delivered code must match.

nodes.label: Spec part: Constraints
nodes.rationale: Constraints: project conventions to follow and things the implementer must not touch.

nodes.label: Spec part: Verification
nodes.rationale: Verification: the command or commands that prove the delivered work actually works — the evidence the architect re-runs before accepting the lane's output.

nodes.label: An unwritable spec is undecided architecture
nodes.rationale: A spec you can't finish writing signals that the decision isn't made yet. That is architect work — not a reason to hand the ambiguity to a cheaper model.

nodes.label: Parallelism rule for independent specs
nodes.rationale: Independent specs — no shared files and no ordering dependency — launch as parallel agents in a single message. Sequential chains and single-file surgery stay serial.

nodes.label: Dual-lane bake-off on one spec
nodes.rationale: For high-stakes work, run `codex-implementer` and `fable-implementer` on the same spec and let the architect pick the stronger diff — two model families, one judged result.

nodes.label: Commitment-boundary consult
nodes.rationale: Consult `fable-advisor` before committing to an architecture, data migration, API shape, or refactor strategy — the moments that decide whether the next hour is wasted. Pass it the decision, the constraints, and the options considered, then act on the verdict or surface the disagreement; never silently ignore it.

nodes.label: Two-resisted-attempts consult trigger
nodes.rationale: Whenever the same problem has resisted two distinct attempts, that is a trigger to consult the read-only `fable-advisor` rather than continue attacking it in-session.

nodes.label: Mandatory end-of-deliverable review
nodes.rationale: Always, once, at the end of a deliverable, the advisor reads the accumulated changes with fresh eyes — against the stated goal rather than the conversation — and returns ship / fix-first / rethink. The architect does not report done before this review.

nodes.label: Same-model reviewer caveat
nodes.rationale: When the deliverable came from `fable-implementer`, the reviewer and the implementer are the same model. The final review is still worth doing because it reads the diff in a clean context against the goal, but it is a fresh-eyes check, not an independent-model check.

nodes.label: Verification discipline: reports are claims, not evidence
nodes.rationale: Before accepting any lane's work the architect reads the diff and re-runs the verification command (or spot-checks its quoted output against the working tree). "Should work", "tests should pass", or a report with no command output means the task is not done.

nodes.label: Corrected spec, not "use your judgment"
nodes.rationale: A lane that reports a spec gap gets a corrected spec, not a "use your judgment". Resolving the ambiguity is architect work, and pushing it down to the lane is how a cheap lane produces expensive rework.

nodes.label: Architect pattern
nodes.author: DannyMac180
nodes.rationale: The plugin's core doctrine: the Claude Code session runs on Opus as a full-time architect that owns requirements, decomposition, specs and verification, routes every implementation task to the right lane, and obtains a Fable 5 review of the finished work before calling anything done. It exploits Claude Code's ability to run each subagent — and the session itself — on a different model.

nodes.label: Opus architect session
nodes.author: DannyMac180
nodes.rationale: The session model is Opus (`/model opus`) and acts only as architect: it writes the spec, picks the lane, reads the returned diff and verification evidence, sends the finished work to fable-advisor, and only then reports done. Opus emits judgment and specs, never the bulk of the code.

nodes.label: Routine lane (codex-implementer)
nodes.author: DannyMac180
nodes.rationale: The default implementation lane: the `codex-implementer` agent runs GPT-5.6 Luna at max reasoning through the OpenAI Codex CLI. Route here when the spec fully determines the outcome — Codex does the typing and emits the bulk of the code.

nodes.label: High-complexity lane (fable-implementer)
nodes.author: DannyMac180
nodes.rationale: The `fable-implementer` agent runs Fable 5 and takes one-off tasks where judgment the spec cannot capture decides the outcome: subtle concurrency, hard debugging, security-sensitive paths, and wide refactors.

nodes.label: Review lane (fable-advisor agent)
nodes.author: DannyMac180
nodes.rationale: The `fable-advisor` agent is a read-only Fable 5 skeptic that reviews and never implements. It is consulted at commitment boundaries and always once at the end of a deliverable, returning a verdict of ship / fix-first / rethink.

nodes.label: Mandatory end-of-deliverable review
nodes.author: DannyMac180
nodes.rationale: The advisor review is required, not optional: the architect sends the accumulated changes to fable-advisor 'always once at the end' and only reports done after that review. v4 made this end-of-deliverable review mandatory.

nodes.label: Commitment boundaries
nodes.author: DannyMac180
nodes.rationale: The consult points where even the architect must get a second opinion: before architecture decisions, migrations and API designs, whenever a problem has resisted two attempts, and (in advisor-only mode) before any refactor touching 3+ files.

nodes.label: Context-clean skepticism
nodes.author: DannyMac180
nodes.rationale: The advisor reads the accumulated diff with fresh eyes, judged against the stated goal rather than the conversation, without the session's accumulated assumptions. That context-clean skepticism is stated to be what the final review buys.

nodes.label: Orchestration skill
nodes.author: DannyMac180
nodes.rationale: The skill the plugin ships: the routing doctrine that teaches the session when to use each lane, plus the cost discipline, the five-part spec contract, and the verification rules. With the session on Opus, asking for work is enough — the orchestration skill routes it.

nodes.label: Cost discipline
nodes.author: DannyMac180
nodes.rationale: The rules that keep expensive-model token volume minimal: emit judgment not volume, keep context lean, reason once then hand off. The architect is told to minimize its own token volume and never type code itself.

nodes.label: Five-part spec contract
nodes.author: DannyMac180
nodes.rationale: The spec format shipped with the orchestration skill that makes context-free delegation safe — i.e. lets a subagent with none of the session's context implement correctly from the spec alone.

nodes.label: Verification rules
nodes.author: DannyMac180
nodes.rationale: The rules in the orchestration skill that keep every lane honest: the architect reads the diff and the verification evidence when a lane's report comes back, and verifies that evidence before accepting any lane's report.

nodes.label: Tokens route by capability
nodes.author: DannyMac180
nodes.rationale: The routing economics: Opus emits judgment and specs, the cheap cross-vendor lane emits the bulk of the code, and Fable — the most expensive model available — is spent only where it changes outcomes, namely the hardest implementations and the final review.

nodes.label: Cross-vendor review by construction
nodes.author: DannyMac180
nodes.rationale: Because the routine lane is a different model family than the architect, cross-vendor review is built into the routing rather than bolted on. Models from one family share blind spots, so an implementation from a different lineage catches what same-family review misses — but the architect and reviewer stay Claude; the routine lane is a producer, not a judge.

nodes.label: Racing two implementers on one spec
nodes.author: DannyMac180
nodes.rationale: For high-stakes work, run `codex-implementer` and `fable-implementer` on the same spec and let the architect pick the stronger diff.

nodes.label: Advisor-only mode
nodes.author: DannyMac180
nodes.rationale: The original, minimal arrangement for skipping the orchestration layer: run the session on Sonnet and consult `fable-advisor` only at commitment boundaries. A typical consult costs cents.

nodes.label: Lite-mode install
nodes.author: DannyMac180
nodes.rationale: One file, 30 seconds: copy `agents/fable-advisor.md` into `~/.claude/agents/` and keep the session on Sonnet, getting advisor consults without the orchestration layer.

nodes.label: Plugin install and update
nodes.author: DannyMac180
nodes.rationale: Installed as a Claude Code marketplace plugin: `claude plugin marketplace add DannyMac180/fable-advisor` then `claude plugin install fable-advisor@fable-advisor`; updated with `claude plugin marketplace update fable-advisor` and `claude plugin update fable-advisor@fable-advisor`. The session is then started as the architect with `/model opus`.

nodes.label: Codex CLI requirement
nodes.author: DannyMac180
nodes.rationale: The `codex-implementer` agent needs the OpenAI Codex CLI installed and authenticated (`npm i -g @openai/codex`, then `codex login`). It invokes GPT-5.6 Luna as `gpt-5.6-luna` with `model_reasoning_effort=max`; GPT-5.6 access may be limited during preview.

nodes.label: Codex lane fails loudly
nodes.author: DannyMac180
nodes.rationale: Without model access, an installed/authenticated CLI, or successful authentication, the codex agent reports `STATUS: unavailable` and never silently falls back to a Claude model; the Fable lanes remain unaffected.

nodes.label: Silent Claude model fallback
nodes.author: DannyMac180
nodes.rationale: If a pinned Claude model is not available on the account, Claude Code silently falls back to the session model, so the pattern degrades quietly rather than erroring — if results feel unremarkable, check the plan.

nodes.label: Model resolution order
nodes.author: DannyMac180
nodes.rationale: Claude Code resolves a subagent's model in this order: `CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL` env var, then the per-invocation `model` parameter, then agent frontmatter, then the session model.

nodes.label: Fable access requirement and downgrade
nodes.author: DannyMac180
nodes.rationale: Requires Claude Code >= 2.1.170 with a subscription that includes Fable 5 (Pro, Max, Team or Enterprise). Without Fable access (e.g. API-key billing), change `model: fable` to `model: opus` in the advisor and implementer files — the same pattern with the Fable roles shifted down to Opus.

nodes.label: Per-subagent model routing (Claude Code only)
nodes.author: DannyMac180
nodes.rationale: Claude Code lets every subagent run on a different model, and lets the session itself run on a different model than its subagents — the capability the whole plugin exploits. It is Claude Code only (CLI, desktop, VS Code, web) and does not work on claude.ai.

nodes.label: Always-on CLAUDE.md directive
nodes.author: DannyMac180
nodes.rationale: To make the doctrine always-on, one line is added to the project's CLAUDE.md: be the architect, minimize own token volume, delegate all implementation through the orchestration skill's routing table (never type code yourself), delegate broad exploration to cheap read-only agents, verify evidence before accepting any lane's report, and get a fable-advisor review before reporting any deliverable done.

nodes.label: Delegate exploration to cheap read-only agents
nodes.author: DannyMac180
nodes.rationale: Part of the always-on directive: broad codebase exploration is delegated to cheap read-only agents rather than performed by the expensive architect session.

nodes.label: v4 routing restructure
nodes.author: DannyMac180
nodes.rationale: v4 restructures the routing: the session architect moves from Fable to Opus, the Grok 4.5 lane is removed, `codex-implementer` becomes the default typing lane, and Fable's premium is refocused on the new `fable-implementer` high-complexity lane plus a now-mandatory end-of-deliverable `fable-advisor` review. The removed Grok lane remains available from the v3.1 tree.

nodes.label: Why not run everything on Fable
nodes.author: DannyMac180
nodes.rationale: You can run everything on Fable and it is excellent, but it is also the most expensive lane per token, and most of a session's tokens are orchestration and implementation mechanics that Opus and the codex lane handle at near-parity. Spend the premium where it changes outcomes.

nodes.label: Not Anthropic's advisor tool
nodes.author: DannyMac180
nodes.rationale: This is not Anthropic's server-side API 'advisor tool' feature: these are plain Claude Code subagents plus a skill — readable, editable, and with no beta flags.

nodes.label: Advisor-executor pattern
nodes.rationale: A multi-agent optimization technique that splits reasoning and execution across two different models instead of routing everything through one: a high-capability advisor model analyzes the problem and produces a structured plan, and a faster, cheaper executor model carries that plan out. In Claude Code this means Fable 5 for planning and Sonnet or Opus for execution, cutting overall token cost while preserving quality on complex tasks.

nodes.label: Fable 5 token budget wall
nodes.rationale: Running Claude Code with Fable 5 on a large refactor, multi-file build, or codebase audit burns the usage allocation fast because the premium model both plans and executes every step — every file read, every code write, every minor formatting decision. Anthropic's rate limits and usage caps reflect the real cost of frontier inference, so the default single-model behaviour is simply wasteful.

nodes.label: Advisor role (Fable 5)
nodes.rationale: The advisor (Fable 5) does the thinking: it analyzes the problem, proposes a structured plan, flags edge cases, and produces a precise specification of what needs to happen. Reasoning is what a frontier model is expensive at and best at — pattern recognition, edge-case identification, and structured reasoning — so its use is concentrated there and nowhere else.

nodes.label: Executor role (Opus or Sonnet)
nodes.rationale: The executor (Opus or Sonnet) does the work: it receives the advisor's specification and executes it — writing code, modifying files, running commands — without re-deriving the strategy from scratch. Following a clear, well-structured plan does not require the same depth of reasoning, so a cheaper model performs it reliably at much lower cost per token.

nodes.label: Architect-and-builders analogy
nodes.rationale: The split is framed as separating the architect from the builders: the architect (Fable 5) draws up detailed plans once, and the builders (Opus or Sonnet) implement those plans across dozens of tasks without the architect needing to be on-site for every nail.

nodes.label: Structured plan as the handoff artifact
nodes.rationale: The advisor must emit its plan as structured output — JSON, YAML, or clearly numbered lists — so the executor can parse it reliably. Being specific about what the plan should contain also keeps the advisor's response compact and actionable; structured plans execute more consistently than prose.

nodes.label: Claude Code --model flag
nodes.rationale: Claude Code supports multi-model workflows through its `--model` flag and structured prompt chaining: `claude --model claude-fable-5` for the advisor phase and `claude --model claude-sonnet-4` for the executor phase. A default model can also be set in the Claude Code configuration file and overridden per session.

nodes.label: Step 1 — start a Fable 5 advisor session
nodes.rationale: Open the project and explicitly invoke Fable 5 for planning only, keeping the prompt focused on producing structured output rather than doing work. The three key constraints are: ask for a plan and not execution, request structured output so the executor can parse it, and be specific about what the plan must contain.

nodes.label: Step 2 — save the advisor output
nodes.rationale: Capture the advisor's plan to a file — Claude Code can write directly to the working directory (e.g. 'Write the output to migration-plan.json in the project root'), or stdout can be piped to a file and referenced in the next step.

nodes.label: Step 3 — launch an executor session with Sonnet
